findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new token-refresh block added to `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` (line 96), but the file's imports do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (only jsforce, RRule, zod, logger, HttpError, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse and types are imported). Since `getClient` is invoked from the constructor, every use of the Salesforce calendar service (event creation, updates, deletions) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, completely breaking the Salesforce integration for all installations, not just those opting into credential sync.

findings.title: Computed zod schema keys collapse to the literal string "[object Object]"
findings.body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. `z.string()` returns a ZodString instance whose `toString()` is `Object.prototype.toString`, i.e. the literal string `"[object Object]"`. Both computed keys are identical, the second overwrites the first, and the resulting schema only validates `access_token: z.string()` plus a meaningless optional `"[object Object]"` property. The stated intent ("assume any property with a number is the expiry") is not implemented at all: the expiry field returned by the sync endpoint (e.g. `expires_in`/`expiry_date`) is neither required nor validated, so an endpoint response missing the expiry silently passes validation and propagates `undefined`/`NaN` expiry values into stored credentials.

findings.title: Sync-mode parsing strips all credential fields and writes a literal "refresh_token" placeholder, corrupting stored credentials
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the response is parsed with `minimumTokenResponseSchema` instead of the app schema. zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so the parse result keeps only `access_token`. Then, because `refresh_token` was stripped, line 26 assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token. In GoogleCalendarService this means the credential written back to the DB via `prisma.credential.update` loses the real `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, and every other field, keeping only `{ access_token, refresh_token: "refresh_token" }`. The next refresh attempt uses the bogus token and fails permanently. The same stripping drops `expires_in` in the Office365 path (leaving the old, already-expired value so `isExpired` is always true and tokens are refreshed on every request) and in Zoom produces `Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = `NaN` persisted as `expiry_date`. Additionally, in the non-sync path the placeholder also overwrites a legitimately absent-but-optional `refresh_token` (Office365's schema declares it optional) with the garbage literal.

findings.title: Sync-mode return value is a raw fetch Response but every caller expects a `.data` property
findings.body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` `Response` object directly. All call sites were written for their provider SDK's response shape and read `res.data` / `tokenInfo.data` (Google: `const token = res?.data` then `token.access_token` → TypeError; hubspot: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` → `Date.now() + undefined * 1000` = NaN; zoho-bigin and zohocrm: `tokenInfo.data.error` → TypeError on undefined). A fetch Response has no `.data`; the body must be consumed via `.json()`/`.text()`. As written, the credential-sync feature crashes or silently corrupts token data in every adapted app the first time a token refresh is attempted. The response is also never checked for `response.ok`.

findings.title: Outbound credential-sync request carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no secret, header, or signature (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET exists but is only used to authenticate the inbound webhook). The self-hosted endpoint therefore cannot verify the request originated from the Cal.com instance, so anyone who can reach the endpoint can request fresh OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users by guessing/enumerating user IDs. At minimum the webhook secret should be sent as a header so the receiving side can authenticate the request.

findings.title: Unvalidated `.parse` and unguarded decrypt/JSON.parse turn bad requests into 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on an invalid body, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (line 57) throws if the ciphertext is malformed or not valid JSON. Neither is caught, so the endpoint returns an unhandled 500 (with stack details in some configurations) instead of a 400 with a meaningful message. The endpoint also has no `req.method` guard, so any HTTP method is accepted. Malformed-input paths of an internet-exposed webhook should return 4xx, not 500.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
findings.body: The shared secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses plain string comparison, which is not timing-safe; other webhook verifications in the codebase/industry use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Also, `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` for repeated headers, which silently fails the comparison. Low practical risk, but this is the sole authentication for an endpoint that can overwrite any user's app credentials.

findings.title: Salesforce token is now refreshed unconditionally on every service construction
findings.body: The new code in `getClient` always POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes the credential row, with no expiry check. `getClient` runs from the class constructor, so every calendar operation (create/update/delete event, contact search) now performs an extra OAuth token round-trip to Salesforce plus a DB write, even when the stored access token is still valid. Previously jsforce refreshed lazily. Beyond the latency/DB churn, Salesforce refresh tokens can be invalidated by excessive refresh frequency.

findings.title: Zoom expiry_date becomes NaN when sync mode strips expires_in
findings.body: After `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema)` runs in credential-sync mode, `newTokens` contains only `access_token` (plus the `"refresh_token"` placeholder) because the minimum schema strips `expires_in`, `token_type` and `scope`. Line 122 then computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` = `NaN`, which is persisted to the credential row. `isTokenValid` (`(token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now()`) returns false for NaN, so the adapter treats the credential as permanently valid and never refreshes again — all subsequent Zoom API calls fail with an expired access token.

findings.title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or token-refresh helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a security-sensitive, unauthenticated-input-handling webhook (secret check, AES decryption, credential upsert) and two shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that alter the token-parsing behavior of ~10 app integrations, yet includes no unit or integration tests (the PR checklist confirms none were added). Several of the defects in this review (schema stripping, raw-Response `.data` access, missing prisma import) would have been caught by basic tests exercising the sync-enabled path and the webhook handler with malformed payloads.
